mss-4ca917a2fe0262406158.text: Varicocele most commonly occurs on the {{c1::left}} side of the body
mss-4ca917a2fe0262406158.extra:
- Because the left spermatic vein enters the left renal vein at a 90° angle, ﬂow is less laminar on left than on right; thus left venous pressure > right venous pressure, resulting in varicocele being more common on the left

- The left renal vein that crosses midline can become compressed between aorta and SMA (Nutcracker Syndrome); presents with gross hematuria, left flank pain, nausea, vomiting; can present with varicocele and varicose veins

mss-70d722924f8378dc8c0c.text: Congenital hydrocele ("communicating hydrocele") occurs due to incomplete obliteration of the {{c1::processus vaginalis}} (infants)
mss-70d722924f8378dc8c0c.extra:
- The processus vaginalis is an evagination of peritoneum that is pulled by the testis as it descends into the abdomen and into the scrotum, this then obliterates to trap and cover a part of the testis

- Failure to obliterate completely results in peritoneal fluid being able to collect in the tunica vaginalis

- These usually resolve spontaneously by 1 year of age; however, patients can develop indirect inguinal hernias later in life


Photo credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mss-d32f85bd3e82bf688061.text:
What major artery must be examined for injury following a clavicular fracture?

{{c1::Subclavian artery}}
mss-d32f85bd3e82bf688061.extra:
- Especially if there's a bruit → CT angiography
- May also damage the brachial plexus
- Middle fractures → conservative treatment
- Distal fractures / unstable fracture → ORIF


“Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.”; Photo credit: English: Nicholas Zaorsky, M.D., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

What additional vascular imaging study is recommended if this noninvasive imaging is abnormal?
- Additional vascular imaging is advised if the ABI is less than 0.9. Formal contrast angiography (FCA), CTA, and duplex ultrasonography are available options (see table below)
- CTA is currently the preferred test (of choice) due to its accessibility, speed, and non-invasiveness
- Formal contrast arteriography is invasive (needs direct femoral artery puncture) and delays management by necessitating the referral to an interventional radiology team

StudyProsCons
CTAQuick, accessible, and non-invasiveSmall/distal arteries are difficult to visualize; an intravenous contrast agent injection is used
Duplex USPrecise, non-invasiveOperator-reliant; not easily accessible
Contrast arteriographyHighly sensitive and specificCostly, time-consuming, and invasive; involves intra-arterial contrast media

InjuryArtery affectedCharacteristics
Dislocations of the shoulder girdleAxillary arterySeizures can cause posterior dislocations, which are more likely to injure the axillary nerve. Axillary artery damage commonly accompany anterior dislocations which are more common
Clavicle fractureSubclavian arteryPatients may also have hemothorax or pneumothorax
Supracondylar fractureBrachial arteryMore frequently affects children and, if ignored, can lead to Volkmann's contracture
Pelvic fractureBranches of internal iliac artery (superior gluteal and internal pudendal)
The superior gluteal artery is more likely to be the source of arterial bleeding when there are severe posterior fractures. Injury to the internal pudendal artery can arise from severe anterior fractures, which is a major source of blood loss.
Both injuries can cause major blood loss and hemorrhagic shock
Hip dislocationFemoral arteryPosterior dislocations manifest as an internally rotated and adducted leg with an increased incidence of sciatic nerve injury. Anterior dislocations present with externally rotated and abducted legs with an increased risk of femoral artery injury.
Also, risk of avascular necrosis if combined with femoral head fracture
Knee dislocationPopliteal arteryPatients with posterior dislocation experience arterial injury more commonly than those with anterior dislocation
Tibial plateau fracturePopliteal arteryPatients with medial injuries get arterial damage more commonly than those with lateral injuries

mss-126e5638c5559b4f9d96.text: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) is an elbow injury that may be due to repetitive {{c2::flexion}} ({{c2::forehand}} shots) that causes tendinosis of the {{c1::pronator teres::muscle}} and {{c1::flexor carpi radialis::muscle}}

mss-28bdd3636a1836ed27b3.text: Lateral epicondylitis (AKA tennis elbow) is an elbow injury that may be due to repetitive {{c1::extension}} ({{c1::backhand}} shots) that causes microtrauma of the {{c2::extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)}} tendon at its origin
mss-28bdd3636a1836ed27b3.extra:
- Backhand strikes transmit sudden, extreme forces through the lateral epicondyle which, over time, may cause microtrauma of the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)
- This microtrauma leads to excess fibroblasts and neovascularization at its origin on the lateral epicondyle
- Results in pain near the lateral epicondyle and worsened pain with resisted wrist extension
- HOWEVER, the pain will also be near proximal wrist extensors, and will worsen with resisted middle finger extension


Photo credit: OpenStax, CC BY 4.0


Photo credit: www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mss-9fa180ee8cb7cfdb4b36.text:
The pathologies associated with {{c1::carpal tunnel syndrome}} may be remembered with the mnemonic "Pressing Down HARD":

Pressing: {{c1::Pregnancy::reproductive circumstance}} (due to edema)
Down: {{c1::Dialysis-related amyloidosis::inflammatory disorder}}

H: {{c1::Hypothyroidism::thyroid disorder}}
A: {{c1::Acromegaly::pituitary disorder}}
R: {{c1::Rheumatoid arthritis::inflammatory disorder}}
D: {{c1::Diabetes mellitus::endocrine disorder}}

It may also be associated with {{c1::repetitive use}}
mss-9fa180ee8cb7cfdb4b36.extra:
Dialysis-related amyloidosis: β2-microglobulin is not effectively removed by dialysis → forms amyloid which deposits in bones, joints, tendons (commonly shoulder and wrist)

Hypothyroidism: increased circulating levels of TSH stimulate fibroblasts in the connective tissue of the carpal tunnel to deposit GAGs; these attract water which cause the carpal tunnel to swell impinging the median nerve

Acromegaly: enlarged hands and feet can lead to compression of the median nerve and carpal tunnel syndrome (up to 1/3 of those with acromegaly get carpal tunnel syndrome)

Rheumatoid arthritis: deposits of antibodies (rheumatoid factor / anti-CCP antibodies) in joints of the wrist results in inflammation of median nerve

DM: circulating advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) deposit in carpal tunnel vessels and cause inflammation, growth of basement membrane, and fibrosis, leading to impingement of median nerve

mss-c893970d39b0b05442c1.text:
Injury to the {{c1::axillary}} nerve ({{c2::C5-C6::nerve roots}}) is commonly due to:

- Fracture at {{c3::the surgical neck of the humerus}}
- {{c4::Anterior dislocation}} of the humerus
mss-c893970d39b0b05442c1.extra:
Fractured surgical neck of humerus
- Common in elderly, nerve runs below humeral head and wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus
- More dangerous than dislocation b/c can disrupt blood supply to the humeral head (anterior / posterior humeral circumflex artery) → avascular necrosis

Anterior shoulder dislocation
- Caused by arm being abducted and extended with a force being applied to arm that originates from behind (posterior)
- e.g., someone blocking a basketball shot, someone tackling while a person is throwing a football

mss-066c9179af86022e50db.text:
Injury to the {{c1::musculocutaneous (C5-7)::nerve and roots}} nerve presents as:

- Loss of sensation over the {{c3::lateral forearm}}

Musculocutaneous nerve innervates the:
- Coracobrachialis (flex and adduct arm at the glenohumeral joint)
- Biceps brachii (supinates the forearm, and flexes the forearm)
- Brachialis (flexes the forearm)
- Some forearm supination is preserved due to the supinator muscle (innervated by the radial nerve)

mss-aa01f4f7d409c204c997.text:
Injury to the {{c1::radial}} nerve ({{c2::C5-T1::nerve roots}}) can be caused by:

- {{c3::Midshaft}} fracture of the humerus
- Compression of the {{c4::axilla}}
- "{{c5::Nursemaids}} elbow"
- Repetitive {{c6::pronation/supination of forearm}}
mss-aa01f4f7d409c204c997.extra:
Midshaft fracture of the humerus
- Damage of the nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus; deep brachial artery is at risk of damage
- Triceps brachii are spared and sensory nerves over posterior arm / forearm are unaffected (nerves that supply these have already been given off); thus supination is the most impacted

Compression of the axilla
- Due to incorrect use of crutches or passing out with arm over chair

Radial head subluxation ("nursemaids elbow")
- Longitudinal traction applied to an extended an pronated arm (e.g., by nursemaid pulling vigorously at childs arm) can lead to annular ligament slipping over the head of the radius and impinging deep radial nerve
- Causes lateral elbow pain, weakness, no sensory deficits or wrist drop

Repetitive pronation / supination:
- Leads to finger drop
- E.g., screwdriver use
- Palsy in deep radial nerve (innervating the extensors of the fingers and wrist)

mss-1c85dba590f02bdce8ed.text:
{{c1::Median}} nerve ({{c2::C5-T1::nerve roots}}) injury is commonly due to:

- {{c5::Anteromedial}} {{c5::supracondylar}} fracture of the humerus ({{c3::proximal::proximal or distal}} lesion)
- {{c4::Carpal tunnel}} syndrome ({{c3::distal::proximal or distal}} lesion)
- {{c4::Wrist}} laceration ({{c3::distal::proximal or distal}} lesion)
mss-1c85dba590f02bdce8ed.extra:
Anteromedial supracondylar fracture of the humerus
- Supracondylar ridges are immediately proximal to lateral / medial epicondyles
- Most common pediatric elbow fracture
- Typically caused by fall on outstretched elbow
- Results in sensory deficits in medial distribution, loss of thumb opposition, flexion of lateral fingers and lumbricals of 2nd / 3rd digits
- Patients have a "pope's blessing" hand sign upon patient making a fist
- Because brachial artery is paired with median nerve here, brachial artery can be damaged resulting in Volkmann's Ischemic Contracture (uncontrolled flexion in hand muscles as flexors become fibrotic and short)
- MRI elucidates

Carpal tunnel syndrome or wrist laceration
- Result in a "median claw lesion" (distal median nerve lesion - test distal lesion by having patients extend from a fist)

mss-02c4abe8a735c252d3c6.text:
Loss of muscle action in a(n) {{c5::median}} nerve injury includes loss of:

1. Wrist {{c1::flexion (weakened)::motion}}
2. Flexion of {{c2::lateral::medial/lateral}} fingers ({{c2::2nd::#}} and {{c2::3rd::#}} digits)
3. Thumb {{c3::opposition::motion}} and thumb {{c3::flexion::motion}}
4. {{c4::Lateral::medial/lateral}} 2 lumbricals ({{c4::2nd::#}} and {{c4::3rd::#}} digits)
mss-02c4abe8a735c252d3c6.extra:
- Wrist flexion is innervated by BOTH median and ulnar nerves. If one is injured, wrist flexion will deviate to the opposite side

- Thumb opposition is median nerve recurrent branch innervated
- Thumb flexion is dual-supplied by two median nerve components (recurrent branch and anterior interosseous)
- Thumb aBduction has median & radial nerve innervation
- Thumb aDduction is innervated by the deep ulnar nerve

mss-78c4824811534d760b7f.text:
Injury to the {{c1::ulnar}} nerve ({{c2::C8-T1::nerve roots}}) commonly occurs due to:

- Fracture of the {{c3::medial epicondyle}} of humerus ({{c4::proximal::distal or proximal}} lesion)
- Fractured {{c3::hook of hamate}} ({{c4::distal::distal or proximal}} lesion) (from fall on outstretched hand - "FOOSH")
mss-78c4824811534d760b7f.extra:
- Fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus results in "OK gesture" lesion (proximal ulnar lesion - test proximal lesion by having them make a fist)

- Fracture of the hook of hamate results in "Ulnar Claw" lesion (distal ulnar lesion - test distal lesion by having them extend fingers from a fist)

mss-673f214c4be092a6d253.text:
Loss of muscle action in a(n) {{c1::ulnar}} nerve injury includes loss of:

1. {{c2::Wrist flexion & adduction::2}}
2. Flexion of {{c3::medial (4th and 5th digits)}} fingers
3. {{c4::Abduction}} AND {{c4::adduction}} of fingers (interossei)
4. Medial two {{c5::lumbricals (4th and 5th digits)}}
mss-673f214c4be092a6d253.extra: This is because the ulnar nerve innervates the flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial portion of the flexor digitorum profundus; once it enters the wrist (between hook of hamate and pisiform bone in Guyon canal) it divides into superficial ulnar and deep ulnar (deep intrinsic hand muscles)

mss-fb78a4d58bed93d5b67a.text: The {{c1::intrinsic hand}} muscles are lost in both {{c2::Klumpke’s}} palsy and {{c2::thoracic outlet}} syndrome
mss-fb78a4d58bed93d5b67a.extra:
- Includes the lumbricals, interossei, thenar, and hypothenar muscles

- Lumbricals are controlled by the median and ulnar nerves

- Interossei and hypothenar muscles are controlled by the ulnar nerve

- Thenar muscles are controlled by the median and recurrent branch of the median nerve

mss-be70d3daceadbbf0e826.text: Loss of the {{c1::lumbricals::specific muscle group}} in {{c2::Klumpke palsy}} results in {{c3::total claw hand}}
mss-be70d3daceadbbf0e826.extra:
MCP joint is hyperextended, DIP and PIP joints are flexed
- At rest, a balance exists between extrinsic flexors/extensors of hand and intrinsic muscles (e.g., lumbrical muscles which flex MCP joints and extend DIP and PIP joints)
- "Clawing" is prominent in distal lesions of the median or ulnar nerves
- Remaining extrinsic flexors exaggerate the loss of lumbrical function

mss-625c3886d0a43359901a.text: {{c1::Winged scapula::Condition}} is due to a lesion of the long thoracic nerve that supplies the {{c2::serratus anterior}}
mss-625c3886d0a43359901a.extra:
- Serratus anterior originates on the surface of the first 8 ribs and inserts on medial border of the scapula

- Functions to stabilize and rotate scapula upward

- Acts with trapezius to rotate glenoid cavity superiorly, allowing complete abduction of arm over head from horizontal position

- Anchors scapula to thoracic cage

Lateral wingingWinged Scapula
(medial winging)

mss-2ee78ee4425c41c8d099.text: Clawing of the hand is characterized by {{c1::<u>extension</u>::flexion/extension}} at the {{c2::MCP}} joint, {{c1::<u>flexion</u>::flexion/extension}} at the {{c2::PIP}} joint, and {{c1::<u>flexion</u>::flexion/extension}} at the {{c2::DIP}} joint

mss-e458d2396e8ecd1ae873.text: Claw hand deficits are {{c2::less::more/less}} pronounced in {{c1::proximal::proximal/distal}} lesions
mss-e458d2396e8ecd1ae873.extra:
Check out the pattern:
- Distal nerve lesion = apparent when extending fingers / at rest
- Proximal nerve lesion = only apparent when asked to make a fist

CDE: Claw hand deficits, Distal lesions, on Extension

mss-fc3724ca2b333440e326.text: {{c1::"Ulnar claw" hand}} (distortion of the hand) is most apparent when {{c2::extending fingers or at rest}}, and is due to a(n) {{c3::distal ulnar}} nerve lesion
mss-fc3724ca2b333440e326.extra:
Loss of either the median or ulnar nerve takes out the lumbricals (flexion at MCP joint) → unopposed flexion of PIP and DIP joints


Mnemonics:
"Distal damage draws digits down"
→ distal lesions cause claw hand, affected fingers remain flexed

"Proximal palsy points phalanges proud"
→ proximal lesions prevent closure of fist, affected fingers remain extended

mss-867b9b3d3d7fe689d352.text:
The tibial nerve is commonly injured due to:

- {{c1::Knee}} trauma
- {{c1::Baker cyst::Proximal lesion}}
- {{c1::Tarsal tunnel syndrome::Distal lesion}}
mss-867b9b3d3d7fe689d352.extra:
- Baker cyst is located in the popliteal fossa, can cause palsy either due to direct compression or indirectly after cyst rupture

- Tarsal tunnel is made by flexor retinaculum and medial surfaces of talus and calcaneus; causes include exercise, flat feet, DM, neurofibromatosis, lipomas

- Weakness of {{c1::intrinsic}} muscles of the foot

- Distal tibial nerve lesions (e.g., at the tarsal tunnel) include tarsal tunnel syndrome

- Motor innervation to the {{c4::gluteus medius}}, {{c4::gluteus minimus}}, and {{c5::tensor fascia latae}}

mss-009f5fcc35e5b201c56e.text: The superior gluteal nerve is commonly injured due to {{c1::intramuscular}} injection to the {{c1::upper medial}} gluteal region (iatrogenic)
mss-009f5fcc35e5b201c56e.extra:
- This is because this area is right by where the superior gluteal nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the level of the piriformis

- Thus inject into superolateral quadrant (anterolateral region) to avoid nerve injury

- The superomedial quadrant has the highest risk of injuring the superior gluteal nerve

mss-a6944f917dc1d65ff86e.text: Injury to the superior gluteal nerve presents with {{c7::Trendelenburg sign}} and a(n) {{c8::gluteus medius::muscle}} lurch
mss-a6944f917dc1d65ff86e.extra:
- Trendelenburg sign is caused by the weakness of the gluteus medius / minimus muscles causing the pelvis to sag toward the unaffected (contralateral) side when the patient stands on the affected leg

- Gluteus medius lurch is seen when walking, as the patient will lean toward the affected (ipsilateral) side to compensate for hip drop

mss-2fd9a570a2c2c7172a10.extra:

- Δ pressure (diastolic blood pressure - ICP) < 30 mmHg (a normal ICP = 0 mmHg); as the ICP pressure rises, it gets closer to diastolic BP - thus a gradient < 30 means that the compartment pressure is super high

- Significant {{c1::long bone}} fractures
- {{c2::Reperfusion}} injury
- Animal {{c3::venoms}}

- Reperfusion injury can be secondary to an arterial thrombosis or crush injury

- Constrictive dressing (splints, casts), or poor surgical positioning can also cause

- Other injuries include thermal injuries and nontraumatic causes (bleeding disorders and vascular disease)

mss-94956d6def09a2fae077.text: {{c1::Plantar fasciitis}} is characterized by sharp {{c3::heel}} pain that is worse in the {{c2::morning}}
mss-94956d6def09a2fae077.extra:
- Classic pain pattern is worse with weight-bearing after periods of inactivity & worse with prolonged standing / walking, but better with normal daily activity

- Patients may have a bony spur at the location of the pain, but removal of the spur is not indicated

- Manage with activity modification, physical therapy, and padded heel inserts

mss-2395419ccb6eca9f98e7.text: Plantar fasciitis is distinguished from tarsal tunnel syndrome in that heel pain in plantar fasciitis {{c1::improves}}* with use
mss-2395419ccb6eca9f98e7.extra:
- Pain in plantar fasciitis improves with normal activity
-*Prolonged standing or walking causes re-emergence of pain

- Pain worsens with use in tarsal tunnel syndrome
- Patients with tarsal tunnel syndrome will have sensory tibial nerve + intrinsic foot deficits, and can be elicited by Tinel Test

mss-55a36a7dad170363449e.text: De Quervain tenosynovitis presents with pain over the {{c1::radial::radial/ulnar}} side of the wrist
mss-55a36a7dad170363449e.extra: Specifically over the radial styloid; pain radiates proximally to the forearm, and distally to thumb

supplements.title: Bootcamp
supplements.html: Watch associated Bootcamp video - Wrist and Hand: De Quervain Tenosynovitis

mss-022c5154054a6aad88ab.text:
In de Quervain tenosynovitis, there is stenosing tenosynovial inflammation of the first dorsal compartment tendons that run over the {{c3::radial styloid}} process, these being the tendons of the:

- {{c1::Abductor pollicis longus}}
- {{c2::Extensor pollicis brevis}}
mss-022c5154054a6aad88ab.extra:
- The wrist has 6 dorsal compartments ordered from radial to ulnar, these deep extensor tendons travel through the most radial compartment marked (#1)

- Abductor pollicis longus is responsible for abducting the thumb at the wrist, while the extensor pollicis brevis extends and abducts the thumb

Photo credit: Henry Vandyke Carter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

supplements.title: Bootcamp
supplements.html: Watch associated Bootcamp video - Wrist and Hand: De Quervain Tenosynovitis

mss-7dd223db09b69cc5b5a9.text: Inflammation of the 1st dorsal compartment in de Quervain tenosynovitis is due to thickening / swelling of the {{c1::extensor retinaculum}}, which causes friction with tendon movement
mss-7dd223db09b69cc5b5a9.extra:
The extensor retinaculum (AKA dorsal carpal ligament) is a thickened part of antebrachial fascia that holds the extensor tendons in place; its friction against the tenosynovial sheath results in inflammation


Photo credit: Σχέδιο: Δρ.Χαράλαμπος Γκούβας, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

supplements.title: Bootcamp
supplements.html: Watch associated Bootcamp video - Wrist and Hand: De Quervain Tenosynovitis

mss-b98a251a2b62b00c0e87.text: Central to the pathogenesis of de Quervain tenosynovitis is repetitive {{c1::wrist}} motion
mss-b98a251a2b62b00c0e87.extra:
- This results in thickening of the extensor retinaculum, causing friction on the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis (muscles that extend and abduct the thumb) resulting in inflammation

- Conservative management (NSAIDs, thumb spica splinting)


Photo credit: Σχέδιο: Δρ.Χαράλαμπος Γκούβας, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

supplements.title: Bootcamp
supplements.html: Watch associated Bootcamp video - Wrist and Hand: De Quervain Tenosynovitis

mss-314f2bfc54b704888579.text: De Quervain tenosynovitis can be diagnosed with the Finkelstein test, in which pain is elicited over the radial styloid with {{c1::ulnar}} deviation of the hand while the {{c2::thumb}} is flexed in the palm
mss-314f2bfc54b704888579.extra:
- Clinical diagnosis - no additional testing / imaging required!

- AKA de Quervain tendinopathy


Image licensed by Physeo and used with permission. Purchase full access here.

mss-cb2c455623cf74910522.text: A ganglion cyst is a(n) {{c1::non-tender::tender/non-tender}} cystic swelling most commonly located on the {{c2::dorsal}} side of the wrist
mss-cb2c455623cf74910522.extra:

mss-b95beecde199c36b8a51.text: Ganglion cysts are often found in association and in communication with {{c1::synovial sheaths}} on the dorsum of the hand
mss-b95beecde199c36b8a51.extra:
- These are the joint / tendon sheaths of the hand
- They are thought to be due to mucoid degeneration of periarticular tissue, leading to outpouching of the connective tissue

mss-93f480168372968398bf.text: Ganglion cysts are most commonly found at the distal attachment of the {{c1::extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)}} muscle
mss-93f480168372968398bf.extra:
- This muscle and the Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus (ERCL) contract to produce abduction / extension of the wrist (radial nerve innervation)
- The ECRB originates from lateral epicondyle and attaches to metacarpals II and III

Photo credit: CFCF, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

mss-56c104721e391a171d57.text: Ganglion cysts arise from {{c1::herniation}} of dense connective tissue
mss-56c104721e391a171d57.extra:
- Associated with mucoid degeneration of periarticular tissue

- These cysts have no true epithelial lining, and can be transilluminated


Photo credit: Kulzerwi, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

mss-15c3814d8769c84e0287.text:
In the elbow there are three joints, these being:

- {{c1::Radiocapitellar}} joint
- Ulnohumeral joint
- {{c2::Proximal radioulnar}} joint
mss-15c3814d8769c84e0287.extra:
- Radiocapitellar is where the radial head articulates with the humeral capitellum

- Ulnohumeral is where the trochlear notch of the ulna articulates with the humeral trochlea

- Proximal radioulnar is where the radial head articulates with the radial notch of the ulna

Is placement of a foley (urethral) catheter contraindicated in urethral injury?

Gallbladder hypomotility is primarily associated with what kind of gallstone?

- Sludge can be supersaturated with either cholesterol or calcium bilirubinate, but cholesterol stones are technically more common (~80%)

mss-df4569fceb6bf19ec518.text: Manually reducible symptomatic internal hemorrhoids (grade 3) are typically treated with {{c1::rubber band ligation}} in the {{c1::out::in or out}}patient setting
mss-df4569fceb6bf19ec518.extra:
- This cuts off their blood supply, causing them to degenerate

- Hemorrhoids are only treated if symptomatic

- Internal hemorrhoids that do not prolapse (grade 1) or are reducible at rest (grade 2) are treated conservatively with lifestyle modification, stool softeners, and/or sitz bath

- Irreducible or thrombosed (grade 4) and/or refractory symptomatic internal hemorrhoids are treated with surgery

mss-d7703ae79254688e302e.text:
Proximal tibial nerve lesions present with:

- Foot {{c1::dorsi}}flexed and {{c1::everted}} at rest
- Loss of foot {{c1::plantarflexion and inversion::2}}
- Weakness of the {{c1::extrinsic}} muscles of the foot
mss-d7703ae79254688e302e.extra:
- The proximal tibial nerve gives off branches that innervate the tibialis posterior (involved in foot inversion), as well as the gastrocnemius / soleus / plantaris muscles (involved in foot plantar flexion)

- Thus patients present with the foot held in the calcaneovalgus position (dorsiflexed / everted)

- Extrinsic foot muscles (e.g., flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus) are also innervated by this part of the nerve (resulting in loss of toe flexion)

- Proximal tibial nerve lesions (e.g., at the popliteal fossa) include knee surgery, baker cyst, and deep penetrating trauma

mss-7d84fd4983e81f67ef1b.text: Circumferential, full-thickness burns can result in eschar formation that restricts venous / lymphatic drainage, leading to {{c1::acute compartment}} syndrome

- Semmes-Weinstein filament testing is the most sensitive method of testing for sensory problems

- Electromyography and nerve conduction studies can be useful in cases where the diagnosis is unclear

mss-4d11bf72d40b2ef31115.text:
What is the next step in management for a patient with suspected mild carpal tunnel syndrome with no thenar or hypothenar atrophy on physical exam?

{{c1::Wrist splinting}}
mss-4d11bf72d40b2ef31115.extra:
- No thenar or hypothenar atrophy on physical exam → not severe disease

- Splinting in neutral position affords the lowest pressure in the carpal tunnel

- Glucocorticoids and/or decompression surgery may be considered in patients with severe disease (significant weakness or refractory symptoms)

- Intial treatment is wrist splinting; second-line is local anesthetic + steroid injection; third-line is surgical intervention

mss-ada3c23d52c5c9c66e7b.text: The palmar cutaneous branch of the {{c1::median}} nerve branches prior to the carpal tunnel, and travels above the transverse carpal ligament
mss-ada3c23d52c5c9c66e7b.extra:
- Supplies skin of the thenar eminence
- Thus, typical carpal tunnel syndrome will not have sensory dysesthesia over the area of the thenar eminence
- Transverse carpal ligament is also known as the flexor retinaculum

mss-c0b8c3b0966ed90121c2.text:
What is the treatment of circumferential burns with evidence of vascular/respiratory compromise?

{{c1::Escharotomy}}

If compartment syndrome develops: {{c1::Fasciotomy}}
mss-c0b8c3b0966ed90121c2.extra:
- Escharotomy: Incision of the burnt necrotic tissue to decrease compartment pressure

- Fasciotomy: Incision of skin, subcutaneous fat, and deep fascia to decrease compartment pressure

- Circumferential burns without vascular/respiratory compromise: elevate + range of motion exercises

mss-55444430069bf6511c82.text:
What pathology presents with an arm that is externally rotated and close to body (handshake position), and numbness over the deltoid?

{{c1::Anterior shoulder dislocation}}
mss-55444430069bf6511c82.extra:
- Managed with closed reduction with sedation

- Numbness is caused by damage to the axillary nerve (C5-C6)

- The handshake position resembles a "shooting gun" pose

- Often results from unstable ligaments

- Increased risk for recurrent dislocation due to labral tears (i.e., Bankart lesion)

- Bankart lesion = damage to the anterior inferior labrum of the glenoid fossa

What is the mechanism of injury and involved tendon in jersey finger vs. mallet finger?

Jersey finger: {{c1::Forced hyperextension of DIP joint (rupture of flexor digitorum profundus tendon)}}

Mallet finger: {{c1::Forced hyperflexion of DIP joint (rupture of extensor tendon)}}
mss-3e9cc394acb2e8eee668.extra:
- Treatment is splinting (minor mallet injury) vs. surgery (jersey finger + severe mallet injury)

- Trigger finger is due to injury that involves the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joint; glucocorticoid injections are attempted if conservative therapy fails

- Think of a mallet flexing down
- Jersey finger: caught in a player's jersey

mss-fa0a4bb2aaaec859a80d.text: The {{c1::anterior talofibular}} ligament is the most common ankle sprain ("low" ankle sprain) and is injured during {{c2::inversion::inversion / eversion}}
mss-fa0a4bb2aaaec859a80d.extra:
- Ankle sprains are the most common type of ankle injury

- A sprained ankle is nearly always an inversion injury, involving twisting of the weight-bearing plantarflexed foot

- The lateral ligament, specifically the anterior talofibular ligament, is more susceptible to injury in ankle sprains because it is weaker than the medial ligament

- In severe cases, the lateral malleolus of the fibula may also be fractured

mss-fc1bb11ef3b74116922a.text: {{c1::Radiculopathy}} is a spinal pathology described as compression of nerve roots causing pain, weakness, and numbness of limbs
mss-fc1bb11ef3b74116922a.extra:

mss-ddd9cb644a4cc097bc7c.text: A(n) {{c1::myelopathy}} refers to damage to the spinal cord
mss-ddd9cb644a4cc097bc7c.extra:
Can be further divided into compressive and non-compressive; this can cause paraplegia (thoracic or lumbar myelopathy) or quadriplegia (cervical myelopathy)

- Myelopathy: spinal cord compression; neurological deficits in upper and lower extremities
- Radiculopathy: affects nerve roots asymmetrically; pain in axial spine radiating through limb
- Mononeuropathy: single peripheral nerve affected by compression, trauma, or vascular causes
- Polyneuropathy: diffuse symmetric dysfunction of peripheral nerves
- Plexopathies (brachial, lumbosacral): multiple peripheral nerves, asymmetric

What are the step-up treatments for a patient with carpal tunnel syndrome?

{{c1::Splint}} → {{c1::steroid injection}} → {{c1::oral steroids}} → {{c1::surgery}}

mss-68f5627b40ea4a7c12b1.text: Reperfusion of a limb following arterio-occlusive ischemia for longer than 4-6 hours can lead to intracellular and interstitial edema with possible {{c1::compartment}} syndrome
mss-68f5627b40ea4a7c12b1.extra:
- The edema compresses blood flow

- Due to increased capillary permeability → interstitial edema → interstitial pressure become greater than capillary pressure → ischemia and necrosis

mss-8aebc0866e9a25a06ab4.text: Compression of the ulnar nerve within the {{c1::cubital tunnel}} results in decreased pinch strength, and decreased sensation over the little finger, medial palmar surface, and medial dorsal surface of the hand
mss-8aebc0866e9a25a06ab4.extra:
- In occupations that involve hammering and lifting heavy objects, such as carpentry, the ulnar nerve can be compressed proximally within the cubital tunnel (cubital tunnel syndrome) as a result of repetitive elbow flexion, which decreases the volume of the cubital tunnel

- May also experience elbow pain that radiates to the forearm

- Compression of ulnar nerve within Guyon canal does not affect dorsal aspect of the hand

mss-0dd816cae63ebda97f68.text:
What is the next step in diagnosis for a stable patient with suspected vertebral osteomyelitis and no focal neurologic deficits?

{{c1::Imaging and biopsy}}
mss-0dd816cae63ebda97f68.extra:
- e.g., X-ray, followed by MRI, followed by CT-guided biopsy

- Confirm the diagnosis through a CT-guided bone biopsy with gram staining, culture, and histology

- This not only confirms the diagnosis but, in conjunction with findings from the blood culture, also enables appropriate antibiotic selection based on the culture results

- vs. empiric antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin + ceftaz/cefepime) for unstable patients

mss-35ebccd708fb0c64c5d9.text:
What imaging may be used as an alternative to MRI for a patient with positive drop arm test?

{{c1::Musculoskeletal ultrasound}}
mss-35ebccd708fb0c64c5d9.extra:
- This patient has a suspected rotator cuff tear

- MSUS is cost-effective, comparable to traditional MRI for rotator cuff tear evaluation, and allows for detailed visualization of specific shoulder regions at rest and during movement

- Typical ultrasound findings of rotator cuff tear include focal hypoechoic/anechoic areas, with evidence of fiber discontinuity, juxtaposed with the hyperechoic fibrillar pattern of undamaged tendon

- US is also used for evaluating the Achilles tendon injuries


Image(s) provided by www.radiologyassistant.nl. Used with permission.

mss-0a71d69294965b10a8f5.text:
What is the treatment of hip dislocation?

Without fracture: {{c1::Closed reduction}}

With fracture: {{c1::Open reduction}}
mss-0a71d69294965b10a8f5.extra: In the absence of fracture, closed reduction should be performed within 6 hours to minimize the risk of osteonecrosis of the femoral head

mss-4b284fe02a9f302b2516.text: Positive forward bend test in an adolescent is highly suggestive of idiopathic scoliosis and should be followed with {{c1::X-ray}} to confirm the diagnosis
mss-4b284fe02a9f302b2516.extra:
- Patient bends at the waist with knees straight to evaluate asymmetry → test may show a "rib hump" (thoracic) or "lumbar hump"

- X-ray is needed to determine the Cobb angle (i.e. the severity of the curve)
